headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: dexter’s broad egress and secrets handling can feed pipecat’s shared-bus, multi-service pipeline by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: dexter can write to .dexter/scratchpad/ and pipecat exposes stdin/stdout plus shared-bus session state. That creates a plausible content-bridging path where dexter-produced text can be consumed by pipecat as instructions. No direct provenance controls are documented for either agent, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF dexter writes attacker-controlled text into .dexter/scratchpad/ and pipecat reads that text from the shared bus or stdin/stdout, injection is possible.
IF pipecat treats upstream text as instructions without provenance tagging, the bridge becomes exploitable.
mitigations: Separate the scratchpad and bus into per-agent directories or topics.
Add a provenance prefix and reject untrusted instruction blocks.
Disable automatic ingestion of dexter outputs into pipecat.
Review one sample handoff for prompt-like content before enabling automation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: dexter handles financial data, market data, and multiple API keys, while pipecat’s shared bus and broad text/audio/video surfaces can propagate that content to external STT/LLM/TTS services. Because pipecat’s default docs list many third-party APIs and dexter has broad network egress, the pair can leak sensitive data unless tightly constrained.
conditions: IF dexter places financial data or secrets into shared state, pipecat can forward them to third-party APIs listed in its docs.
IF both agents run under the same workspace or bus, sensitive text can traverse from dexter into pipecat outputs.
mitigations: Remove secrets from any shared bus payloads.
Route only redacted summaries from dexter to pipecat.
Disable external STT/LLM/TTS providers for sensitive sessions.
Use separate credentials and workspaces per agent.
Add a quick DLP check on shared messages.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: dexter has broad network egress and file access to .dexter/scratchpad/, while pipecat supports multiple instances with shared bus state and many outbound service integrations. The overlap is not a proven same-directory write conflict, but both can mutate shared runtime state and external resources, so coordination bugs are plausible in default-style deployments.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same workspace or shared bus, state races can occur.
IF either agent updates shared external resources without locking, last-writer-wins conflicts are possible.
mitigations: Assign distinct workspaces and API credentials.
Serialize writes through one coordinator.
Turn on per-resource locking where available.
Keep pipecat instances isolated by session.
Audit one shared resource path for concurrent writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: dexter is an autonomous execution agent, and pipecat is a real-time voice/chat framework that can pass text through LLM and transport services. If pipecat consumes dexter output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream actions or user-facing speech without verification. The default pipeline shape makes this dangerous.
conditions: IF pipecat forwards dexter-generated text into an LLM, TTS, or transport step without verification, errors propagate.
IF downstream automation acts on that text, the cascade can become user-visible or operational.
mitigations: Insert a verification step between dexter and pipecat.
Require citations or structured outputs from dexter.
Block direct action-taking from unreviewed text.
Log and sample-check one end-to-end turn.
Use a human approval gate for high-impact outputs.

E_compliance.rationale: dexter explicitly touches financial data and market data and requests multiple API keys, while pipecat can send text/audio/video through many third-party services and analytics endpoints. That creates a compliance mismatch risk around retention, residency, and vendor sharing. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined data flow, not either one alone.
conditions: IF regulated financial data is routed through pipecat’s third-party services, retention and vendor-sharing obligations may be triggered.
IF the deployment requires stricter residency or logging controls than pipecat’s defaults, compliance gaps emerge.
mitigations: Map each data class to an allowed provider list.
Disable analytics and unnecessary third-party services.
Set short retention on logs and transcripts.
Review vendor DPAs before enabling sensitive flows.
Use separate pipelines for regulated and non-regulated data.
